Tiger King & Queen - Pumba Zoo

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How did a couple build a hundred-animal Zoo in Mbombela without a permit?

Unique Selling Point:
Drone footage of the controversial Pumbaa Wildlife Park on the outskirts of the city will show over a hundred animals, including lions and tigers, in steel cages with no shelter or shade.
Footage of 50 breeders and exporters meeting with attorney Macbeth Ncongwane with the express purpose of mounting a legal challenge to prevent Ban Animal Trading and other animal rights groups from accessing information from provincial environmental authorities through PAIA. This group have "donated" a R100 000 retainer to Macbeth Attorneys to represent them. Macbeth is a spokesperson for the Pumbaa Zoo and refers to the venture as "we".

Summary:
Melanie and Hennie Maritz have spent over R7 million on the planned Pumbaa Zoo in Mbombela. Neither Melanie (former loan shark arrested by the Hawks in 2013, and owner of MS Funerals) nor husband Hennie (builder and owner of M&H Lowveld Properties) have any experience in the management of wild animals. They currently have over a hundred wild animals on the property, housed in steel cages with no shelter or shade.
Their plan is to import other exotic animals including bears and to open a Zoo for education, environmental awareness and entertainment. They will also build lodges for accommodations of paying guests.
A petition against the Zoo has attracted over 10 000 signatures. The argument is that with the Kruger national park on their doorstep, there is no need to imprison wild animals in cages.
Pumbaa's lawyer Macbeth Ncongwane (twice sanctioned and fined by the Law Society) says that is "privilege" talking. How are poor, underprivileged children from the townships meant to get to the KNP? However the KNP does run programmes for under-privileged children to access the Park.

Further information:
Pumbaa Zoo does not have the necessary permits to open.
1. No permit has been granted by the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Association.
2. PAAZA has not received an application from Pumbaa, nor have they inspected the facility.
3. Mbombela Municipality received NO application for the Zoo to operate, yet one has been granted.
4. Were the necessary permits obtained to transport over a hundred animals to the Zoo?
5. Two cheetahs are being bought from HESC at R20 000 each.
6. The attending vet claims to have sterilised all the animals at the Zoo. What will he do with the cheetahs?
7. The constitutional right to access information held by government is going to be challenged by Macbeth Ncongwane, on behalf of all wildlife exporters mentioned in BAT's investigations. He has somehow convinced them that this is a cause they can win and they have been asked to donate R5000 each.

Extra Budget Items:
An extra shoot day in Johannesburg to interview BAT, John Werth from PAAZA and the NSPCA who have objected to the Zoo.

We will need 2 days in Mbombela to interview Macbeth Ncongwane, the MTPA, Liezl de Jongh the local conservationists who blew the whistle on the Zoo, the Municipal Manager, as well Hennie and Melanie Maritz. We also need to take a tour of the Zoo and film the animals. Please bear in mind that it is a 4 hour drive from Johannesburg to Mbombela.

Car hire and fuel to travel to Mobombela and back.
Accommodation for Producer and Presenter for one night in Mbombela.
S&T for two for 1 night.

Script:


PUMBAA ZOO

V/O: A vicious catfight has broken out in the Lowveld. In August the citizens of Mbombela discovered on Facebook that their city is about to get a private Zoo.

Liezel: We don’t need a Zoo. We don’t want animals in cages. All the other ones are failing in this country, so we don’t see why there is a need for another one.

V/O: When local animal activist, Liezel de Jongh was sent photos of the cages, she posted them on Facebook.

Liezel: I asked does anybody know what this is for, and I also asked if they knew who the owners were? The owners almost immediately commented and they told me I will hear from their lawyer.

V/O: The owners are Hennie and Melanie Maritz. Hennie is a builder who renovates and sells houses. Melanie owns Masibambisane Funeral Society with branches throughout Mpumalanga. Their self-funded, private Zoo called Pumbaa Wildlife Park has been established on the outskirts of town at a cost of R8 million.

Boy: Zoological gardens are a legal thing to have.

V/O: Boy Nobunga is the CEO of the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency – the provincial authority that approved the establishment of the Zoo.

Boy: When you submit your application, there would then be inspections and everything to check before the management plan is approved, because it’s on the basis of the approval of the management plan that you can then be in the process to establish a zoo.

Mac: Having looked at the management plan and having done the inspection would you say all environmental legislation was complied with while they were erecting the zoo?

Boy: Yes, we were satisfied. They put in the request and we gave them pre-approval on the 3rd of July.

Link: One of the major criticisms of the new Zoo is the fact that the Kruger National Park is down the road. Why put wild animals in cages when you can go and see them in their natural environment?

V/O: Almost 10 000 people have signed an online petition against Pumbaa Zoo which was established without the knowledge of the Mbombela Municipality. This 12-hectare farm was already zoned for agricultural use, so no Environmental Impact Assessment was required, The municipality will only get involved once the Zoo, with adjacent guest lodge and restaurant, opens to the public next year says Joseph Ngala.



Joseph; There obviously will have to be a public participation process. We've also since been petitioned as a municipality. But our stance is that we can't even entertain this because we have not been approached neither by MTPA nor by the developers. As a city currently there's nothing on our table.

V/O: Hennie and Melanie Maritz wouldn’t speak to us but invited us to the Zoo to interview their lawyer. We arrived half an hour early on a surprisingly chilly day but got an even colder reception from Hennie. He chased us off the property and told us to wait outside the gate. The reason for this soon became apparent – we had jumped the gun and missed the scheduled demonstration.

Mac: So it’s ten minutes to go before we do our interview and it looks like the support team has been brought in. Nothing like a nice welcoming party, right?

V/O; A dozen vehicles arrived, bringing locals to show their support for a Zoo in Mpumalanga. On arrival they were given T-shirts and placards and seemed a bit unsure of what to do next. Some said they’d been told there may be job opportunities in future. This man already has a job with Melanie Maritz.

Mac: Who said you should come here? Who invited you?

Employee: Who invited me? The manager.

Mac: Who is your manager?

Employee: Mrs Melanie.

Mac: Mrs Melanie?

Employee: Mrs Melanie.

Mac: Oh, she said you must come here?

Employee: Yes.

Mac: To support the zoo?

Employee: Yes.

Mac: So you’re not working today?

Employee: No.

Mac: Ok, and they told you they’d give you T-shirts and food?

Employee: Yes.

V/O: This man gave his name as Ephraim Lekwadu, and said the demonstration was advertised on Facebook.

Mac: Who posted it on Facebook that you must come here?

Ephraim: No, no they didn’t call us to come here. We just decided that today there’s going to be a topic for the Zoo.

Mac: Yes but who told you that there’s going to be a topic here?

Ephraim: Here? Facebook gave the date, it’s the 20th.

Mac: And then transport who arranged it?

Ephraim: What?

Mac: The transport?

Ephraim: We arranged it ourselves to come here.

V/O: But Ephraim Lekwadu, the man who happened to see this on Facebook, also happens to be in business with Hennie Maritz in Likwadu Services.

Pumbaa’s lawyer, Macbeth Ncongwane duly arrived and was greeted at the gate by his client Hennie, who then invited us back inside.

Macbeth: From a point of privilege one won’t understand why do you need a zoo. But a zoo serves a very important purpose for the people of Nelspruit and Mpumalanga.

V/O: Macbeth claims the Zoo will be more accessible to the underprivileged.

Macbeth: With less than R200 they will be able to come here and see all the animals that they are likely not to see in Kruger. You can travel the whole day sometimes in the Kruger you will never see a lion.

Macfarlane: How far is this place from the nearest township?

Macbeth: It’s about thirty.

Macfarlane: 30kms? So it almost costs the same then, to go from the nearest township to Kruger or from the township to here. Why isn’t it built closer to the township if it’s really for the underprivileged?

Macbeth: No, I differ with you. Kruger has no accessibility for an ordinary, underprivileged person from the township. There are no taxis going to Kruger. But here it's gonna be very viable because from town it's about 15 minutes, 5 minutes-drive to here to come and have a look and satisfy yourself with all the animals, and it gives you educational experience, experiential, and also I think entertainment.


Smaragda: Kruger National Park offers many programs for the underprivileged children specifically, and for the communities who live around the Kruger National Park.

V/O: Smaragda Louw from Ban Animal Trading is fiercely opposed to all zoos.

Smaragda: They are remnants, and anachronistic remnants, of a past that we should really just try and forget. It's absolutely horrific, and we don't want to go there anymore. Animals are not commodities. They are not things that people need to walk past, stare at for like literally two seconds and then walk on. We have no right to do that to animals.

V/O: There are now 142 animals at the Zoo including lion, white lion, leopard, hyena and jackal. There are also exotic species like Bengal tiger, Siberian tiger, jaguar and puma.

Macbeth: All these animals are bred locally. The Siberian tiger is bred locally, the jaguars are bred locally. The wildlife breeders are breeding in all corners of South Africa, so the animals are not used to any other environment other than South Africa.

Link 2: The final written approval for Pumbaa Zoo was given in July. The conditions are clear: No Breeding, No Trading. But this means the animals are being sterilized.

John: Sterilization of animals so soon seems strange, but it’s a management decision.
V/O: John Werth is the Executive Director of PAAZA, the Pan-African Association of Zoos and Aquaria. They are the accreditation body dedicated to improving the standard of Zoos in Africa to meet international criteria. Pumbaa Zoo has applied for membership, but John seemed baffled by their sterilization policy.
Mac: Is that what normally happens in zoos? Is that what you have seen?

John: No. That is their decision. Mostly, in zoos you have endangered and critically endangered species. Zoos and aquariums become the facilities to hold the assurance populations so that that population does not go extinct.

V/O: Pumbaa Zoo also has seven wild dogs – an endangered species that appears on the TOPS list of Threatened or Protected Species. The male wild dogs were sterilized on the 18th of September.

Mac: Why would you sterilise an endangered species?

Macbeth: Unfortunately we were given the final approval that says no breeding. So we accept that.

Douglas: As a threatened or protected species you’d be trying to increase the gene pool, and yet here you would be reducing the gene pool. So in terms of a conservation aspect that doesn’t make sense at all.

V/O: Douglas Wolhuter is the Manager of the NSPCA’s Wildlife Protection Unit.

Douglas: The NSPCA are opposed to wildlife in captivity unless there’s a bona fide conservation purpose for it.

V/O: There is another bone of contention regarding the Wild Dogs. The Zoo was provisionally approved in February, but the MTPA stipulated that no animals could be introduced before final written approval. That was only granted in July. However, the NSPCA happened to be inspecting the Zoo on the 17th of June and witnessed the arrival of the Wild Dogs.

Macfarlane: The animals – did they arrive before or after July?

Macbeth: Before.

Macfarlane: They arrived before July?

Macbeth: Yes, after we got pre-approval.

V/O: But when he realised we had the official documents, he contradicted himself.

Macfarlane: So on the 1st of February the MTPA boldly said you may not purchase, transport, introduce or keep animals in the enclosures until final written approval is given.

Macbeth: Yes, 100%. We followed that to the letter.


Macfarlane: Is this not then the basis of them going to the NPA saying that you’ve broken the law?

Macbeth: I don’t think so. All animals that were introduced here came after the final approval, which was the 3rd of July. No animals came between February.

Macfarlane: Between February and July no animals came in at all?

Macbeth: My instructions are no animals came here.

V/O; We then asked about the wild dogs. Melanie Maritz appeared with a file containing all the permits for the animals.

Macfarlane: Ok, so when did the wild dogs arrive?

Macbeth: In terms of the permit issued by the Mpumalanga Tourism Parks Agency it’s 2020/08/10, that’s when the wild dogs were introduced. The permit was issued in August. The final written approval was the 3rd of July, so the animals were brought here after this permit was issued. Otherwise there was no way we would have brought these animals here.

V/O: But when we said we knew they arrived on the 17th of June, he then claimed he’d misread the date.

Macbeth: Oh it’s 6, that’s better. I thought it was 8.

Macfarlane: The permit conditions said you couldn’t have the animals until final approval is given.

Macbeth: Oh no, no , no, no, no, no, no, no you see Mac. If they give you a permit in June, it means they’ve changed their minds about the conditions of your place.

V/O: But the CEO of the MTPA strongly disagrees.

Boy: You can’t do any activity before pre-approval which is the 3rd of July. We have already indicated that some of the matters have been referred to the NPA. We also saw those discrepancies.

V/O: Ironically, Macbeth now accuses animal rights groups of breaking the law.

Link: Ban Animal Trading has become the bugbear of wildlife traders nationwide. Their reports continually expose who is exporting which animals to where. In a bid to stop this information being made public the exp orters have now engaged a lawyer to fight their cause: Enter Macbeth.

V/O: At this meeting held in September in Limpopo, Hennie and Melanie Maritz introduced Macbeth Ncongwane to dozens of wildlife breeders and traders from around the country. Their aim is to stop animal rights groups accessing their permit information.

Macbeth: This is not a banana republic. You can’t just go into a Department and bribe officials, gets permits.

Macfarlane: How do you know that they bribe though? Is there evidence to show that they did?

Macbeth: What would be the other way of getting this information without PAIA? They must show me a PAIA application. Other than that, they obtained it surreptitiously or illegally.

Macfarlane: Who are these specific activists?

Macbeth: It’s EMS Foundation and Ban Animal Trading. They issued a video as well as an investigation report. All the permits – and I represent those clients – they say we never consented for that information to be given out.

V/O:: Both EMS Foundation and Ban Animal Trading deny ever bribing officials for information, and provided copies of some of their Public Access to Information or PAIA requests.

Smaragda: We have a PAIA Act for a reason. Why are we not allowed to hold people accountable when it comes to animals? It’s in the public’s interest to know what is happening to the animals; not only the indigenous ones, but the exotic animals in South Africa. It’s a public interest matter.

V/O: BAT”s latest PAIA application is to the MTPA for information about Pumbaa Zoo.

Macbeth: You can’t have my management plan! The management plan cost R350 000. So, I just give it to you so that you can use it elsewhere? It’s not right.

Boy: Well MTPA when it comes to public access to information we are clear. Everybody who wants information - you follow the rule book - we give you whatever information you require, and we would encourage all other people to do the same. With organs of State you don’t have an option.

Smaragda: They just want to continue with whatever they’re doing – happily - with nobody asking any questions and I’m sorry, we are not going to keep quiet. We are there to speak up, because the animals don’t speak human and we are required – it’s our duty - to do what we are doing.

But here it's gonna be very viable because from town it's about 15 minutes, 5 minutes-drive to here to come and have a look and satisfy yourself with all the animals, and it gives you educational experience, experiential, and also I think entertainment. Smaragda: Kruger National Park offers many programs for the underprivileged children specifically, and for the communities who live around the Kruger National Park. V/O: Smaragda Louw from Ban Animal Trading is fiercely opposed to all zoos. Smaragda: They are remnants, and anachronistic remnants, of a past that we should really just try and forget. It's absolutely horrific, and we don't want to go there anymore. Animals are not commodities. They are not things that people need to walk past, stare at for like literally two seconds and then walk on. We have no right to do that to animals. V/O: There are now 142 animals at the Zoo including lion, white lion, leopard, hyena and jackal. There are also exotic species like Bengal tiger, Siberian tiger, jaguar and puma. Macbeth: All these animals are bred locally. The Siberian tiger is bred locally, the jaguars are bred locally. The wildlife breeders are breeding in all corners of South Africa, so the animals are not used to any other environment other than South Africa. Link 2: The final written approval for Pumbaa Zoo was given in July. The conditions are clear: No Breeding, No Trading. But this means the animals are being sterilized. John: Sterilization of animals so soon seems strange, but it’s a management decision. V/O: John Werth is the Executive Director of PAAZA, the Pan-African Association of Zoos and Aquaria. They are the accreditation body dedicated to improving the standard of Zoos in Africa to meet international criteria. Pumbaa Zoo has applied for membership, but John seemed baffled by their sterilization policy. Mac: Is that what normally happens in zoos? Is that what you have seen? John: No. That is their decision. Mostly, in zoos you have endangered and critically endangered species. Zoos and aquariums become the facilities to hold the assurance populations so that that population does not go extinct. V/O: Pumbaa Zoo also has seven wild dogs – an endangered species that appears on the TOPS list of Threatened or Protected Species. The male wild dogs were sterilized on the 18th of September. Mac: Why would you sterilise an endangered species? Macbeth: Unfortunately we were given the final approval that says no breeding. So we accept that. Douglas: As a threatened or protected species you’d be trying to increase the gene pool, and yet here you would be reducing the gene pool. So in terms of a conservation aspect that doesn’t make sense at all. V/O: Douglas Wolhuter is the Manager of the NSPCA’s Wildlife Protection Unit. Douglas: The NSPCA are opposed to wildlife in captivity unless there’s a bona fide conservation purpose for it. V/O: There is another bone of contention regarding the Wild Dogs. The Zoo was provisionally approved in February, but the MTPA stipulated that no animals could be introduced before final written approval. That was only granted in July. However, the NSPCA happened to be inspecting the Zoo on the 17th of June and witnessed the arrival of the Wild Dogs. Macfarlane: The animals – did they arrive before or after July? Macbeth: Before. Macfarlane: They arrived before July? Macbeth: Yes, after we got pre-approval. V/O: But when he realised we had the official documents, he contradicted himself. Macfarlane: So on the 1st of February the MTPA boldly said you may not purchase, transport, introduce or keep animals in the enclosures until final written approval is given. Macbeth: Yes, 100%. We followed that to the letter. Macfarlane: Is this not then the basis of them going to the NPA saying that you’ve broken the law? Macbeth: I don’t think so. All animals that were introduced here came after the final approval, which was the 3rd of July. No animals came between February. Macfarlane: Between February and July no animals came in at all? Macbeth: My instructions are no animals came here. V/O; We then asked about the wild dogs. Melanie Maritz appeared with a file containing all the permits for the animals. Macfarlane: Ok, so when did the wild dogs arrive? Macbeth: In terms of the permit issued by the Mpumalanga Tourism Parks Agency it’s 2020/08/10, that’s when the wild dogs were introduced. The permit was issued in August. The final written approval was the 3rd of July, so the animals were brought here after this permit was issued. Otherwise there was no way we would have brought these animals here. V/O: But when we said we knew they arrived on the 17th of June, he then claimed he’d misread the date. Macbeth: Oh it’s 6, that’s better. I thought it was 8. Macfarlane: The permit conditions said you couldn’t have the animals until final approval is given. Macbeth: Oh no, no , no, no, no, no, no, no you see Mac. If they give you a permit in June, it means they’ve changed their minds about the conditions of your place. V/O: But the CEO of the MTPA strongly disagrees. Boy: You can’t do any activity before pre-approval which is the 3rd of July. We have already indicated that some of the matters have been referred to the NPA. We also saw those discrepancies. V/O: Ironically, Macbeth now accuses animal rights groups of breaking the law. Link: Ban Animal Trading has become the bugbear of wildlife traders nationwide. Their reports continually expose who is exporting which animals to where. In a bid to stop this information being made public the exp orters have now engaged a lawyer to fight their cause: Enter Macbeth. V/O: At this meeting held in September in Limpopo, Hennie and Melanie Maritz introduced Macbeth Ncongwane to dozens of wildlife breeders and traders from around the country. Their aim is to stop animal rights groups accessing their permit information. Macbeth: This is not a banana republic. You can’t just go into a Department and bribe officials, gets permits. Macfarlane: How do you know that they bribe though? Is there evidence to show that they did? Macbeth: What would be the other way of getting this information without PAIA? They must show me a PAIA application. Other than that, they obtained it surreptitiously or illegally. Macfarlane: Who are these specific activists? Macbeth: It’s EMS Foundation and Ban Animal Trading. They issued a video as well as an investigation report. All the permits – and I represent those clients – they say we never consented for that information to be given out. V/O:: Both EMS Foundation and Ban Animal Trading deny ever bribing officials for information, and provided copies of some of their Public Access to Information or PAIA requests. Smaragda: We have a PAIA Act for a reason. Why are we not allowed to hold people accountable when it comes to animals? It’s in the public’s interest to know what is happening to the animals; not only the indigenous ones, but the exotic animals in South Africa. It’s a public interest matter. V/O: BAT”s latest PAIA application is to the MTPA for information about Pumbaa Zoo. Macbeth: You can’t have my management plan! The management plan cost R350 000. So, I just give it to you so that you can use it elsewhere? It’s not right. Boy: Well MTPA when it comes to public access to information we are clear. Everybody who wants information - you follow the rule book - we give you whatever information you require, and we would encourage all other people to do the same. With organs of State you don’t have an option. Smaragda: They just want to continue with whatever they’re doing – happily - with nobody asking any questions and I’m sorry, we are not going to keep quiet. We are there to speak up, because the animals don’t speak human and we are required – it’s our duty - to do what we are doing. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): How did a couple build a hundred-animal Zoo in Mbombela without a permit?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Drone footage of the controversial Pumbaa Wildlife Park on the outskirts of the city will show over a hundred animals, including lions and tigers, in steel cages with no shelter or shade. Footage of 50 breeders and exporters meeting with attorney Macbeth Ncongwane with the express purpose of mounting a legal challenge to prevent Ban Animal Trading and other animal rights groups from accessing information from provincial environmental authorities through PAIA. This group have "donated" a R100 000 retainer to Macbeth Attorneys to represent them. Macbeth is a spokesperson for the Pumbaa Zoo and refers to the venture as "we".
metadata.Summary: Melanie and Hennie Maritz have spent over R7 million on the planned Pumbaa Zoo in Mbombela. Neither Melanie (former loan shark arrested by the Hawks in 2013, and owner of MS Funerals) nor husband Hennie (builder and owner of M&H Lowveld Properties) have any experience in the management of wild animals. They currently have over a hundred wild animals on the property, housed in steel cages with no shelter or shade. Their plan is to import other exotic animals including bears and to open a Zoo for education, environmental awareness and entertainment. They will also build lodges for accommodations of paying guests. A petition against the Zoo has attracted over 10 000 signatures. The argument is that with the Kruger national park on their doorstep, there is no need to imprison wild animals in cages. Pumbaa's lawyer Macbeth Ncongwane (twice sanctioned and fined by the Law Society) says that is "privilege" talking. How are poor, underprivileged children from the townships meant to get to the KNP? However the KNP does run programmes for under-privileged children to access the Park.
metadata.Further information: Pumbaa Zoo does not have the necessary permits to open. 1. No permit has been granted by the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Association. 2. PAAZA has not received an application from Pumbaa, nor have they inspected the facility. 3. Mbombela Municipality received NO application for the Zoo to operate, yet one has been granted. 4. Were the necessary permits obtained to transport over a hundred animals to the Zoo? 5. Two cheetahs are being bought from HESC at R20 000 each. 6. The attending vet claims to have sterilised all the animals at the Zoo. What will he do with the cheetahs? 7. The constitutional right to access information held by government is going to be challenged by Macbeth Ncongwane, on behalf of all wildlife exporters mentioned in BAT's investigations. He has somehow convinced them that this is a cause they can win and they have been asked to donate R5000 each.
metadata.Extra Budget Items: An extra shoot day in Johannesburg to interview BAT, John Werth from PAAZA and the NSPCA who have objected to the Zoo. We will need 2 days in Mbombela to interview Macbeth Ncongwane, the MTPA, Liezl de Jongh the local conservationists who blew the whistle on the Zoo, the Municipal Manager, as well Hennie and Melanie Maritz. We also need to take a tour of the Zoo and film the animals. Please bear in mind that it is a 4 hour drive from Johannesburg to Mbombela. Car hire and fuel to travel to Mobombela and back. Accommodation for Producer and Presenter for one night in Mbombela. S&T for two for 1 night.
